explain.say: A chimp picks a suitable twig or stem, strips off its leaves and trims it to length. That is not just using a tool but making one, with a plan in mind.

explain.say: It pokes the tool into a termite mound, waits for soldier termites to bite on, then draws it out and eats them. Young chimps learn by watching their mothers for years, and different chimp groups have different tool traditions.

explain.say: New Caledonian crows are tool experts too, making hooks from twigs and cutting stepped probes from tough leaves to winkle grubs out of holes. Sea otters use stones to crack shells, and some dolphins wear sponges to protect their snouts.

faq.q: Do animals make tools or just use them?
faq.a: Some really make them. Chimpanzees strip and trim sticks for termite fishing, and New Caledonian crows shape hooks from twigs and cut probes from leaves, changing objects to suit a job.
Jane Goodall, in 1960, at Gombe in Tanzania. She saw a chimp she called David Greybeard poking grass stems into a termite mound and pulling out termites to eat.
asks: When did we learn chimps use tools?

faq.a: New Caledonian crows snap off a forked twig, trim it and carve the fork into a hook with their beak. In a famous lab test, a crow called Betty bent a straight wire into a hook to lift a bucket of food.

Sea otters crack shellfish on stones, some dolphins carry sea sponges to protect their snouts while foraging, veined octopuses carry coconut shells as portable shelters, and Egyptian vultures throw stones at ostrich eggs.

faq.q: Do young animals learn tool use?
faq.a: Yes. Young chimpanzees watch their mothers for years and can take several years to master cracking nuts with stones. Young crows learn tool skills while staying with their parents.
asks: How do chimps learn to use tools?
Is tool use instinct or learned?

facts: Jane Goodall first saw a chimpanzee fishing for termites with a stem at Gombe, Tanzania, in 1960.
A New Caledonian crow called Betty bent a straight wire into a hook to lift food in a lab test (Weir and colleagues, 2002).
